cocolog: myprog_step/4 -- prefix every predicate you define
why: There is no module system. `:- module/2' is accepted and IGNORED, and the eight vendored SWI libraries are consulted into the same store. Consult appends, so your clauses join theirs in one shared predicate record.
fix: prefix the head with the program's own name

swi: memberchk(X,[X|_]).  sort/2  format/2  findall/3  write/1  is/2
why: Dispatch is construct -> C builtin -> module C half -> knowledge base, short-circuited. A C-registered name never reaches the store, so your clauses are dead code that listing/1 will happily show.

cite.anchor: nobody's builtin: the knowledge base decides

fix: prefix the head

cocolog: never define these, at any arity
why: 22 names are control constructs matched by interned id before the builtin table and before the store. Redefinition is dead code that no check in the language can see.
fix: prefix the head

why: A DCG head occupies arity+2, so `digit//1' is `digit/3' in the store -- which is dcg_basics' own. A blocklist built by a regex over heads is under-broad in exactly the arity that collides.
fix: prefix the non-terminal

cocolog: "abc" IS [97,98,99] BY DEFAULT -- set the flag, or write 'abc'
why: double_quotes DEFAULTS to codes, so a bare "abc" is a code list. All four of SWI's values are settable now -- codes, chars, atom, string -- and the flag really changes what the reader builds, so `:- set_prolog_flag(double_quotes, string).' at the head of a file makes every "..." in it a string. The flag is per-MACHINE, not per-module: it is forced back to codes across a module load, so a program's choice cannot reach inside the vendored SWI files, which are written for codes.

cite.anchor: set_prolog_flag: double_quotes takes codes, chars, atom or string

fix: set the flag, or write 'abc', or str("abc") into a serialiser

why: retract/1 is a C builtin: deterministic, leaving no choice point to fail back into. The failure-driven loop removes exactly ONE clause. retractall/1 was rewritten in this repository for precisely this.
fix: recurse instead of failing back

cocolog: between/3, member/2, select/3, sub_atom/5, clause/2, current_predicate/1 and nth0/3 DO backtrack
why: They are Prolog clauses in a library's Prolog half, not C table entries. The rule is structural: C table => deterministic; clauses => backtracks.

cite.anchor: between(L, H, X) :- L < H, M is L + 1, between(M, H, X).
sub_atom(A, B, L, Aft, Sub) :- atom(Sub), !

swi: a defensive ! on every clause to force determinism
cocolog: omit it where the first arguments are distinct; keep it where the caller may leave argument 1 unbound
why: First-argument indexing is live, and it is a semantics fact here rather than a speed one: a predicate whose first arguments are distinct leaves no choice point. A cut added to force determinism the engine already gives you prunes solutions on the calls where argument 1 IS unbound.
halt/0 sets `halted', and the engine tests halted BEFORE the empty-continuation test -- so the goal reports no solution and run/-s exit 1 with nothing on stderr, indistinguishable from failure.
fix: let main succeed; the CLI's exit code is the verdict

why: Those names are not prefix operators, so the file does not even PARSE. Only dynamic, discontiguous, meta_predicate and multifile are declared at 1150 fx.
fix: delete the directive

fix: delete the directive

cocolog: nothing -- it is tier 1 as dcg_basics
why: library(Dir/Name) becomes the path "Dir/Name", and the vendored file is lib/swipl/dcg_basics.pl. As a directive it is silently ignored; as a GOAL it raises.
fix: delete the directive

why: findall/3,4, forall/2, aggregate_all/3, bagof/3, setof/3 and with_output_to/2 run a NESTED engine that copies an error out as a message and drops the ball. The outer catch never fires and the query ends.
fix: put the catch INSIDE the nested goal

why: A library or loader failure is the NON-ISO error(cocolog_error(Text), _) and does not match error(T, context(_,_)) at all -- the first argument is the wrong shape. See row C3 for what the second argument actually holds.
fix: match error(T, _), and match cocolog_error/1 explicitly

swi: assuming error/2's context is always context(Name/Arity, _)
cocolog: a builtin leaves it UNBOUND; the house style puts a bare Name/Arity there
why: MEASURED, not read: catch(atom_codes(_,_), error(T,context(_,_)), true) DOES catch, because an unbound second argument unifies with anything -- so SWI's pattern is not broken for builtin errors. It is broken for a library that throws the house form error(type_error(a,b), my/2), which context(_,_) cannot match. Card row C2 stated this the other way round and is corrected here.
empirical: cocolog --local query "catch(atom_codes(_,_), error(T,context(_,_)), true), write(caught(T)), nl"  ==>  caught(instantiation_error)
fix: match error(T, _) and never depend on the second argument's shape

cocolog: atan(Dy/Dx) plus a quadrant fix; log(N)/log(B); there is no random
why: An unknown arithmetic FUNCTOR goes through coco_fail_err: -1, no ball, uncatchably fatal. (An unknown arithmetic ATOM like inf raises a catchable type_error(evaluable, inf) instead.)
fix: compute it from the one-argument form

why: A cell is a u64 with 3 tag bits and an INT is v<<3|2 with NO range check. Silent wrap at 2^60.

cocolog: the INTEGER 1024; ** and ^ are the same operation
why: An integer base with a non-negative integer exponent stays integer, and ^ reads the same table entry. Force a float with float(...).
fix: wrap in float/1 if you wanted a float

why: cocolog's write_canonical/1 KEEPS operators -- it passes ignore_ops as 0, making it identical to writeq/1.
fix: write_term/2 with ignore_ops(true)

cocolog: there is no depth limit and no portray
why: Only quoted(true) and ignore_ops(true) are read; every other option is silently ignored rather than refused, because an option a writer does not implement is not a reason to fail a program.
A list cell is './2' here, not SWI 7's '[|]'/2.

swi: --> Codes with a bound code list in the body
why: A body item that is a VARIABLE is a call: it translates to phrase(Cs,S0,S), which calls a predicate named after the list's head rather than emitting the list.
fix: write the two-clause walk

cocolog: the predicates all exist now; "abc" is still a CODE LIST
why: The string type is real: string/1, string_concat/3, split_string/4, sub_string/5, atom_string/2, string_to_atom/2, number_string/2, string_codes/2, string_chars/2, term_string/2, text_concat/3, string_length/2 and string_lower/upper all answer, and a code list is accepted anywhere text is wanted. What the READER does is a flag: double_quotes DEFAULTS to codes, so "abc" is [97,98,99] and string("abc") is FALSE in a file that said nothing, where SWI says true. `:- set_prolog_flag(double_quotes, string).' at the head of a file changes that for the rest of it -- the flag takes all four of SWI's values -- so a string is either MADE or asked for, never written by default.

cite.anchor: set_prolog_flag: double_quotes takes codes, chars, atom or string

fix: atom_string(abc, S) to make one; "abc" is still codes

swi: open/3,4  close/1  read/1  read_term/2,3  nl/1  write/2  current_output/1
why: format/3 takes a SINK, not a stream. The read path is read_file_to_codes/2 and a DCG. (see/1, seen/0, tell/1 and told/0 are absent too, and are left out of this pattern because they are ordinary words: `seen(X)' is somebody's own predicate far more often than it is Edinburgh I/O.)
fix: read_file_to_codes/2 plus a DCG; format/3 with a sink

swi: setup_call_cleanup/3 predsort/3 numbervars/3 nb_current/2 assertion/1 freeze/2 dif/2 when/2 call_with_inference_limit/3
cocolog: absent; the last is deliberately spelled call_limited/3
why: Deliberately absent so ported code errors instead of silently differing: SWI's call_with_inference_limit leaves the goal's choice points alive and call_limited/3 commits to the first solution, and a predicate that agrees with SWI until it does not is worse than one that never claimed to.
fix: write it out, or call_limited/3

cocolog: fails -- four flags answer: executable, argv, os_argv, double_quotes
why: There is no flag table. FOUR flags answer -- executable, argv, os_argv and double_quotes -- and every other one FAILS, so a portability shim written against current_prolog_flag/2 takes the wrong branch, silently. double_quotes is the only one a program can also SET; the other three are questions about the process.
fix: do not branch on a flag

cocolog: write the bytes as codes; write 1000000
why: None of them is in the reader's escape set, and each is a syntax error refusing the WHOLE file rather than the one term.
fix: write the codes out

swi: assuming a :- use_module(library(tcp)). header loaded something
why: The directive hook maps every non-zero return to success -- including the -1 that means `not found on the library path' -- so a missing library makes the directive succeed in TOTAL SILENCE. The absence surfaces much later as existence_error(procedure, tcp_listen/2), naming the predicate and not the module.
empirical: a file whose only directive is use_module(library(no_such_library_at_all)) runs to completion with EMPTY stderr and exit 0; the same term as a goal raises cocolog_error('... not found on the library path')
fix: probe as a goal inside catch/3

swi: current_predicate/1 as an availability probe for a library
cocolog: catch existence_error around the real call
why: current_predicate/1 is about the KNOWLEDGE BASE, and a module's predicates are not clauses in it -- so it says no for a library that is loaded and working. The same flag is what makes the collision oracle work.
fix: call it and catch existence_error

swi: one long clause, or one big atom asserted
cocolog: chunk at <= 3800 bytes and assert the completion mark in the same turn
why: A row must fit inside a page: measured, a clause of 8013 characters stores and 8014 comes back `allocation overflow'. It USED to be worse than the documented refusal -- the throw arrived at COMMIT and took every other clause of the transaction with it, and under --embed the writing process reported nothing at all: exit 0, empty stderr, and the clause simply not there when the next process looked. Since 1.1.0 the store refuses it on the way in, one clause at a time and named, so `assertz/1' raises resource_error(clause_length) and a consult reports it and carries on; since 1.2.0 the budget is derived rather than fixed -- `page - 190 - len(kb) - len(name)', measured at three page sizes and three name lengths -- and the embedded engine is asked its page while a server's is assumed to be the default 8192 unless $COCOLOG_PAGE_SIZE says otherwise. This rule's own 7800 sits below all of that on purpose: a linter has no store to ask. THE ADVICE IS UNCHANGED: a clause this long still cannot be stored, and an error you have to catch is not a place to put a design. A single term over 65535 bytes fails earlier and differently, in the client.

cite.anchor: a Text of 8192 comes back as `allocation overflow'
a Text is limited to 65535 bytes
WHAT A ROW WILL HOLD, MEASURED AND NOT GUESSED

fix: chunk it
empirical: cocolog --embed ./KB run t.pl main, with t.pl holding big('x' x N). Bisected 3000/4000/5000/6000/7000/7500/7900/8000/8010/8011/8020/8100: the clause TEXT stores at 8013 characters and is refused at 8014. Before 1.1.0 both writes exited 0 with empty stderr and N>=8020 read back as existence_error(procedure, big/1); now the write raises error(resource_error(clause_length), _) and the clauses asserted beside it are still there for the next process.
